title: Freedom (CCC 1730–1733)
hookLine: true freedom grows the more we choose the good

cards: Sit someone who has never touched a piano in front of one. Are they free to play anything? In one sense, yes: nobody's stopping them, and they can press any key they like.
But they can't play a single song. Now seat a pianist who has practiced every day for twenty years. Same keys, and she's free to play almost anything: Bach, jazz, a song she makes up on the spot.
Which of them is freer? The Catholic Church says the pianist, and builds a whole idea of freedom on that answer.

teach.h: LEFT IN THE HAND OF HIS OWN COUNSEL.
teach.b: It starts with a gift. The Catechism opens with a line from the book of Sirach, which Catholics count as Scripture, in the Douay-Rheims: "God made man from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel."
God doesn't make puppets. He makes people who can say yes or no, even to him.

teach.h: THE POWER TO ACT, OR NOT.
teach.b: The Catechism describes freedom as a power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act, to do this or that, and so to shape your own life. People are responsible for what they freely choose.
Here's the surprise: the more a person does what is good, the freer they become.
Like the pianist, every good choice is practice, and practice opens up what you're able to do.
A Dominican teacher named Servais Pinckaers called it freedom for excellence, next to the thinner idea of freedom as just picking between options. It runs the other way too.
Jesus says in John's Gospel: "whosoever committeth sin, is the servant of sin." The Catechism calls choosing evil an abuse of freedom that leads to slavery.
Watch a habit take over, the phone late at night, the drink, the lie that needs another lie, and the pattern shows: the more it's done, the less it's chosen.

teach.h: THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.
teach.b: The same chapter holds the promise: "the truth shall make you free." Catholics don't see freedom and goodness as rivals. Goodness is what freedom is for.

how: Catholics are taught that freedom is a gift for choosing the good, and some practice it through daily examination of conscience and small acts of self-discipline, especially in Lent.

doing whatever you want with no limits
the power to choose the good, growing with use

games.q: a beginner and a pianist of twenty years sit at the same piano. which one does Catholic teaching call freer?
o: the beginner, who has no habits at all.
the pianist, whose practice lets her play almost anything.
neither: the keys are the same.
games.why: for the Catechism, freedom grows as we choose the good, the way skill grows with practice.

practice: Find one small place in your day where you usually go on autopilot: the second scroll, the sharp reply, the thing you always put off.
Picture the moment, then picture choosing differently, on purpose, not because you have to but because you can. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to choose it.

wordCard.voice: Freedom. In Catholic teaching, not just picking between options, but the power to choose the good, a power that grows the more it's used.

orig.note: Greek: freedom, the word Paul uses for the liberty Christ gives.

carryVoice: Your line: freedom grows. Just ask the pianist at the keys. That's three hundred nine days now.
